## Data as a Conflict Resolution Mechanism

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decisions, which inherently disrupts top‑down, hierarchical decision‑making. When a company becomes data‑literate, well‑formulated questions and careful investigation invite discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. This environment replaces the stereotype of management‑led hunches with decisions grounded in user data collected through multiple techniques: A/B testing, ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, usability research, and more. Such grounded data is less risky than relying on individual executives’ gut feelings.

A foundational 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” captured this principle. The acronym HIPPO stands for “Highest Paid Person’s Opinion.” The underlying mechanism is that data resolves conflicts without resorting to rank, hierarchy, or company politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, illustrated how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation: when everyone can point to evidence, decisions are depersonalized and more voices can contribute.

## Netflix’s Data‑Literate Culture

Patty McCord, Chief Talent Officer at Netflix for over 12 years, emphasized that a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for customers allows more people to have a voice in product development. At Netflix, the practice of leveraging data was universally accepted—from CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt down to individual contributors. This wasn’t merely top‑down endorsement; it was embraced throughout management and teams.

A critical distinction is that even the CEO does not get to override data with personal preference. McCord noted that any employee, including executives, can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates this by subjecting everyone’s ideas to the same rigor. For example, when Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he would submit it to A/B testing just like anyone else. On rare occasions he might dictate the exact way an idea would work, but only on “his test cell”—the experimental group he backed. That cell would be tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If it didn’t win, it didn’t launch. This mechanism reinforced that ideas, prototypes, features, and flows are all subject to grounded review through experimentation, and that “failing” is a positive outcome. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process as individual teams strengthened the practice across the company.

## Shifting to a Data‑Aware Framework

If an organization is trying to move toward a data‑aware framework, it must examine how product and design decisions have been made historically. When decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, those people need to understand and recognize the value of bringing user data into the process. A key caveat: they may find that their personal weight is diminished, just as any individual opinion’s weight is reduced. This is not a loss of authority but a shift toward collective, evidence‑based decision‑making. The same self‑check applies to anyone advocating for data: are you comfortable and willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process? Without this willingness, the environment cannot fully support data‑driven practices.

## Data-Driven Decision-Making Over Hierarchy

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decisions, thereby breaking hierarchical decision-making structures. A data-literate environment invites discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong, rather than top-down, hunch-based management. Data collected through diverse methods—A/B testing, ethnographic research, prototypes, surveys, usability studies—provides a less risky foundation than individual executives’ gut feelings. An early 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” captured this principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank or company politics.

## Netflix’s Culture of Experimentation

John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, Chief Talent Officer at Netflix for over 12 years, emphasized that a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for customers gives more people a voice in product development. The practice was universally accepted: it started with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt, but was embraced by everyone from management to individual contributors. At Netflix, even the CEO does not get to do whatever he wants; ideas are subjected to the same rigorous A/B testing. When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he would submit it to his own test cell, which competed against other cells proposed by the product team. If his cell didn’t win, it didn’t launch. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas to grounded experimentation and accepting “failure” as a positive outcome.

## Shifting to a Data-Aware Framework

To move toward a data-aware environment, examine how product and design decisions have been made historically. If decisions were concentrated in one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of bringing user data into the process, because the weight of any individual opinion—including their own—will be diminished. Designers and product leaders should also ask themselves whether they are comfortable with data changing the weight of their own opinions in the development process.
